subject: chemistry
question_text: Write on the allotropy of carbon.

mark_split.label: Allotropy and the forms of carbon

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, IPE STUDY MATERIAL for Jr. Students — Chemistry (2026-27 edition), book p.110, chapter 9 p-BLOCK ELEMENTS GROUP 14, Long Answer Questions question 43. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints no per-step allocation on any answer in this chapter. The book prints no exam-appearance years for this question, so appearances[] is empty. THE CRYSTALLINE FORMS: the book names diamond and graphite as the crystalline allotropes and calls fullerene the third form of carbon; NCERT counts diamond, graphite and the fullerenes as crystalline, so this card treats all three. The two-item answer is not an error. BOND LENGTH: the source book prints the graphite C–C distance as 141.5 pm in one place and as 1.42 Å in two others; those are the same value rounded differently, and this card prints 141.5 pm only. Neither form is an error. SPELLING CORRECTED: the source prints 'Diamond dyes are used for drawing thin wires'; the word is 'dies' — a die is the tool a wire is drawn through — so this card writes 'diamond dies'. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: Allotropy and the forms of carbon
lines: Allotropy is the existence of an element
in two or more forms in the same
physical state, differing in physical
properties but having the same chemical
properties. The forms are allotropes.
Carbon shows allotropy.
Crystalline forms: diamond and graphite,
and the fullerenes such as C₆₀, which
are also counted as crystalline.
Amorphous forms: coal, coke, animal
charcoal, lamp black and gas carbon.
steps.why: A long answer needs a plan on the page before the detail starts. Defining allotropy and then splitting carbon's forms into crystalline and amorphous tells the reader what the rest of the answer is going to cover and in what order.
common_mistakes: Starting straight at diamond. The word allotropy has to be defined, because that is what the question is about.
Putting coal or coke among the crystalline forms. Those are the amorphous forms of carbon.
steps.memory_tip: Crystalline: diamond, graphite, fullerene. Amorphous: coal, coke, charcoal, lamp black, gas carbon.
steps.margin_note: Write the definition and the two lists first; they are the plan for the whole page.

steps.label: Diamond — structure
lines: In diamond each carbon atom is sp³
hybridised and is bonded to four other
carbon atoms.
The four bonds point to the corners of
a regular tetrahedron.
The pattern repeats in all three
directions, so the whole crystal is one
giant covalent network.
steps.why: Every property of diamond in the next step is read off these lines: four bonds per carbon, fixed directions, and a network that never ends in a molecule. Writing the three numbers here means they do not have to be repeated later.
common_mistakes: Giving the bond angle as 120°. That is graphite's angle; diamond's is 109°28′.
Calling diamond a molecular solid. There are no separate molecules; the crystal is one covalent network.
steps.memory_tip: Diamond: sp³, four bonds, 154 pm, 109°28′, 348 kJ mol⁻¹.
steps.margin_note: Put the three numbers on their own lines; they are easy to read back.

steps.label: Diamond — properties and uses
lines: Diamond is the hardest known substance,
because its network is rigid in three
dimensions and has no sliding layers.
It has a very high melting point,
because melting it means breaking
covalent bonds throughout the crystal.
It is a bad conductor of electricity,
because all four valence electrons are
used in bonds and none is free.
It has a very high refractive index, so
a cut stone shines brightly and is used
as a gem.
It is used as an abrasive, for cutting
glass, in drilling bits, and in diamond
dies for drawing thin wire.
steps.why: Each property is written with the structural reason beside it, so the answer explains rather than lists. Hardness, melting point and the lack of conduction all come out of the same network, and the gem use is the one property that does not — it comes from the refractive index.
common_mistakes: Writing that diamond conducts electricity. It has no free electrons, so it is a bad conductor.
Writing 'diamond dyes' for the wire-drawing use. A die is the block with a hole through which the wire is drawn, so the word is die.
steps.memory_tip: Hard, high melting, no conduction, high refractive index — the first three from the network, the last from the optics.
steps.margin_note: Give the reason beside each property; a bare list of properties does not answer the question.

steps.label: Graphite — structure
lines: In graphite each carbon atom is sp²
hybridised and is bonded to three other
carbon atoms by sigma bonds.
These bonds build flat sheets of
hexagonal rings, stacked one above
another.

lines.text: C–C bond length in a sheet = 141.5 pm

lines: The fourth valence electron of each
carbon is delocalised over the sheet.
The sheets are held together only by
weak van der Waals forces.
steps.why: Graphite differs from diamond in two ways only, and both are on these lines: one bond fewer per carbon, which leaves a delocalised electron, and weak forces between the sheets instead of a network in the third direction.
common_mistakes: Writing that the sheets are joined to each other by covalent bonds. Only weak van der Waals forces act between the sheets.
Answering sp³ for graphite. Each carbon is bonded to three others, so it is sp².
steps.memory_tip: Graphite: sp², three bonds, 141.5 pm, 120°, one delocalised electron.
steps.margin_note: Name the delocalised electron and the weak forces; the next step is built on both.

steps.label: Graphite — properties and uses
lines: Graphite is soft and greasy, because a
small sideways force overcomes the weak
forces and one sheet slides over the
next.
It conducts electricity, because the
delocalised electrons move along the
sheets.
It has a high melting point, because
the bonds inside the sheets are strong
covalent bonds.
It is used as a lubricant and in pencil
leads.
It is also used for crucibles that must
stand great heat, for electrodes, in
electroplating, and as a moderator in
nuclear reactors.
steps.why: The two headline properties of graphite come from two different parts of its structure, and they must not be swapped: the sliding sheets make it a lubricant, and the delocalised electron makes it a conductor. The high melting point is added because it shows the sheets themselves are strongly bonded.
common_mistakes: Giving the sliding layers as the reason for the conduction. The layers explain the lubricant property; the delocalised electron explains the conduction.
Writing that graphite has a low melting point because it is soft. Its melting point is high; the softness comes from the sliding sheets.
steps.memory_tip: Sheets slide, so it lubricates. Electrons move, so it conducts.
steps.margin_note: Keep the two reasons apart; swapping them is easy to do.

steps.label: Fullerene
lines: The fullerenes are the third crystalline
form of carbon. The best known is C₆₀,
called buckminsterfullerene or a bucky
ball.
C₆₀ is a closed cage built of twenty
six-membered rings and twelve
five-membered rings.
A six-membered ring may share an edge
with either a six-membered or a
five-membered ring, but a five-membered
ring shares its edges only with
six-membered rings.
The cage has 60 vertices, with one
carbon atom at each vertex.
Each carbon is sp² hybridised and makes
three sigma bonds; its fourth electron
is delocalised, so C₆₀ has aromatic
character.
There are two C–C distances in C₆₀:
It is made by heating graphite strongly
in an electric arc under helium or
argon.
steps.why: Fullerene carries two marks here because it needs a shape, a ring count, a bonding description and a preparation. The ring rule is the part easiest to forget, and it is what makes the cage close: a sheet of six-membered rings alone stays flat, as it does in graphite.
common_mistakes: Swapping the ring counts. There are twenty six-membered rings and twelve five-membered rings.
Writing that two five-membered rings share an edge. A five-membered ring shares its edges only with six-membered rings.
Giving one C–C distance for C₆₀. There are two, 143.5 pm and 138.3 pm.
steps.memory_tip: Twenty six-membered rings, twelve five-membered rings, sixty vertices, sixty carbon atoms.
steps.margin_note: Give the ring counts and the rule about which rings may share an edge; both are part of the structure.

steps.label: Relative stability

lines.text: Graphite is more stable than diamond

lines: Graphite is thermodynamically more
stable than diamond, even though
diamond is the harder of the two.
Heated to 1800–2000 °C in a vacuum,
diamond changes into graphite.
All of these forms are the same
element, carbon. Only the way the atoms
are joined is different, which is what
allotropy means.
steps.why: Hardness and stability are two different things, and a student who assumes the hardest form must be the most stable has the relationship backwards. Closing with the definition again ties the three structures back to the one word the question asked about.
common_mistakes: Writing that diamond is the more stable form because it is harder. Graphite is thermodynamically the more stable of the two.
Saying diamond changes into graphite on ordinary heating. The change needs 1800–2000 °C in a vacuum.
steps.memory_tip: The harder form is not the more stable one: graphite is.
steps.margin_note: One closing line naming the stability and the element completes the answer.

insider_note: This is a survey question, so a complete answer covers all three crystalline forms — diamond, graphite and fullerene — with the structure of each and the properties that follow from it.
